Disastrously muddled in concept, incoherent and clumsy, pointlessly overviolent for trashy effect, sometimes unintentionally risible and often poorly sung, Annilese Miskimmon's production is all the more worrying for being created by one of the people who actually runs ENO.
Few stagings have been as vague – if not actually misguided – about when and where the action takes place.
After all, this bold version of Tosca could be viewed as an exhilarating operatic The Spy Who Loved Me : it has a licence to thrill.
The audience is appreciative, though overall my feelings are mixed.
And that’s the story of this Tosca, a fine idea overpowered by a stalled and bland set design that leaches its power.
The production is just too unanchored to succeed.
This Tosca is an opera for our time.
There is no doubting the political punch of this Tosca, whose thrust remains true to the spirit and soul of Puccini’s opera.
Puccini’s masterpiece emerges as urgent, human and devastatingly relevant.
The ticket price is worth it for the altered ending alone.
The pounding, passionate score emerges as the unchallenged victor of the evening.
Ultimately, the evening carried Tosca’s true message: that great music, performed with supreme artistry, always triumphs.
In short, a busy, agenda-driven production impressing most for much superlative music making.
It does not quite rescue a production that, for all its updating, feels less like a step forward than a sideways shuffle into a bigger room.
Musical compensations are few but rewarding, led by Ben Glassberg’s terrific conducting, drawing a ripe sound from ENO’s excellent orchestra and sensitive to the needs of his cast.
Annilese Miskimmon's new staging is the sixth I've encountered at the Coliseum, and easily the worst.
Miskimmon’s Tosca is an enjoyable and accessible production, complete with spectacular (unspoiled) ‘shocks’, excellent performances and modern commentary.
The standout performance comes from the ENO orchestra under Ben Glassberg, who embody every ounce of the majesty of Puccini's score.

cn.t: ENO's politically reimagined Tosca in a contemporary Eastern European setting divides critics: some praise Glassberg's conducting and the production's fresh urgency, while others find the concept overwrought and the staging confused.
